before.title: History and Physical
before.content: The client was brought to the ED early morning today, accompanied by his daughter. 6L oxygen via face mask was applied and peripheral IV was inserted enroute to the hospital. The client's chief complaint is shortness of breath. The client finds it difficult to complete sentences due to respiratory distress. He has a history of poorly controlled primary hypertension for 15 years due to medication non-adherence. Client also has history of myocardial infarction (MI) 5 years ago. Current medications include lisinopril. He is a smoker for over 40 years; used to smoke 5-10 cigarettes a day, but cut down to 2-3 cigarettes since his MI.

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 08:00 - Client's breathing remains labored. Productive cough noted with small amounts of pink-tinged frothy sputum. Distended jugular veins observed when head of bed is elevated to 45 degrees. Abdomen appears slightly distended; client reports a feeling of fullness and bloating. Right upper quadrant tenderness noted on palpation, suspect hepatomegaly. Edema in lower extremities now assessed as 2+ pitting dependent edema.

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 0845:The parent brought the client to the hospital after finding the client in the bathroom vomiting and unable to stand without assistance. The client states that she has experienced sore throat and nasal congestion for the past week. She reports 4 episodes of emesis during the past 24 hours and abdominal pain that is diffuse, constant, non-radiating, and rated 3 on a scale of 0-10. The client also reports polydipsia and polyuria over the past 2 months. The last menstrual period ended approximately 6 weeks ago with no abnormalities. Pregnancy status is unknown. The client is taking no medications, and she reports no smoking, alcohol, or recreational drug use. Family history includes hypertension and diabetes mellitus. The client appears drowsy and is oriented to person and time only. The abdomen is soft without guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness, and bowel sounds are normal. No blood is present in emesis. Respirations are rapid and deep. Breath sounds are clear. Vital signs are T 37.1° C), P 128, RR 30, and BP 88/60 mm Hg. Finger-stick blood glucose level is 33.3 mmol/L.

before.title: Laboratory Results
before.content:
Laboratory Test and Reference Range          0900

Glucose, serum (random)
<11.1 mmol/L                                                     31.8 mmol/L

Potassium
3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L                                              5.7 mmol/L

before.title: Prescriptions
before.content:
0905:

- Monitor blood glucose level every hour
- Initiate 0.9% sodium chloride 125 mL/hr IV
- Administer regular insulin IV continuous infusion
- Maintain NPO status except for oral medications
- Administer 0.9% sodium chloride 1000 mL IV bolus
- Initiate 50% dextrose solution IV PRN for hypoglycemia

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 0830:Client presents to employee health clinic appearing visibly exhausted with dark circles under eyes and clenched jaw. Client reports working 65–70 hours weekly over the past 4 months due to administrative restructuring, high-stakes student disciplinary hearings, and upcoming provincial accreditation reviews. He describes persistent, band-like tension headaches across the forehead and occiput, progressive midday fatigue, and profound insomnia, waking up nightly around 0300 with racing thoughts. Over the past 2 weeks, to maintain focus and combat sleep loss, he increased caffeine intake from 1 morning coffee to 5–6 espresso shots daily and began self-medicating with over-the-counter ibuprofen 800 mg orally 3 to 4 times daily on an empty stomach. He now reports worsening gnawing, burning epigastric discomfort that intensifies shortly after drinking espresso. Medical history: no personal history of chronic illness; denies tobacco or illicit drug use; social alcohol use (1–2 beers on weekends, none recently). Family history: father diagnosed with essential hypertension at age 48 and suffered an acute myocardial infarction at age 58.

Medical history: no personal history of chronic illness; denies tobacco or illicit drug use; social alcohol use (1–2 beers on weekends, none recently). Family history: father diagnosed with essential hypertension at age 48 and suffered an acute myocardial infarction at age 58.

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 0800:Arthur Vance, a 58-year-old male, presents for evaluation of persistent, daily retrosternal burning (heartburn) and acidic regurgitation for over 12 years. Over the past 18 months, symptoms have intensified despite self-medicating with over-the-counter antacids; he reports occasional difficulty swallowing tough meats. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 38 years (~38 pack-years) and reports a chronic morning cough productive of tenacious grey-white mucus. He notes progressive exertional shortness of breath when climbing more than one flight of stairs. Medical history: essential hypertension diagnosed 7 years ago, poorly adherent to prescribed medications; denies history of myocardial infarction or stroke. Orthopedic history: sustained a right tibial fracture 4 years ago requiring 10 weeks of rigid cast immobilization; he recalls his right calf was visibly shrunken, weak, and thin compared to the left upon cast removal, which gradually improved with physical therapy rehabilitation.

before.title: Diagnostic Reports
before.content:
Upper Endoscopy (EGD) & Mucosal Biopsy:
Esophagitis with salmon-pink mucosal tongues extending 3.5 cm circumferentially above the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsy confirms Barrett's esophagus with intestinal metaplasia (stratified squamous epithelium replaced by glandular columnar epithelium containing goblet cells). Focal areas demonstrate low-grade dysplasia with cellular pleomorphism, nuclear enlargement, and hyperchromatism, without invasion through the basement membrane.

Bronchoscopy & Endobronchial Biopsy:
Right and left mainstem bronchi demonstrate erythematous, friable mucosa with loss of glistening ciliated surface. Biopsy reveals squamous metaplasia: respiratory ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium has been replaced by multi-layered stratified squamous epithelium.

Transthoracic Echocardiogram:
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). Interventricular septal wall thickness: 1.5 cm (reference: 0.6–1.1 cm). Left ventricular posterior wall thickness: 1.4 cm (reference: 0.6–1.1 cm). Estimated ejection fraction: 58%. Grade I diastolic dysfunction consistent with chronic systemic arterial hypertension.

He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 38 years (~38 pack-years) and reports a chronic morning cough productive of tenacious grey-white mucus. He notes progressive exertional shortness of breath when climbing more than one flight of stairs. Medical history: essential hypertension diagnosed 7 years ago, poorly adherent to prescribed medications; denies history of myocardial infarction or stroke. Blood pressure today is 124/78 mmHg on ramipril 10 mg daily. Reflux symptoms have completely resolved on esomeprazole 40 mg daily. Repeat surveillance EGD with targeted biopsies reveals intact mucosal lining without dysplastic progression. Repeat spirometry shows improved FEV1.

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 0900:Elena Rostova, a 46-year-old female, is admitted accompanied by her sister. Her sister reports that Elena has consumed 1 to 2 bottles of wine daily for the past 12 years, with intake escalating over the past 6 months following acute personal stress. For the past 4 weeks, her nutritional intake has been severely compromised, subsisting almost entirely on alcohol and processed crackers. Over the past 10 days, she developed progressive right upper quadrant heaviness, scleral icterus, dark amber urine, and generalized weakness. Medical history: no known history of viral hepatitis, biliary disease, or diabetes. Medications: none; denies taking acetaminophen, prescription medications, or intravenous drugs. Physical examination: alert but slow to respond; sclerae and sublingual mucosa visibly jaundiced; firm, smooth, tender hepatomegaly palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin. No asterixis or peripheral edema noted.

before.title: Laboratory & Pathology
before.content:
Serum Chemistry & Hepatic Enzymes:
• AST (Aspartate Aminotransferase): 284 U/L (Reference: 10–40 U/L)
• ALT (Alanine Aminotransferase): 142 U/L (Reference: 7–56 U/L) [AST:ALT ratio = 2.0]
• Total Bilirubin: 3.8 mg/dL (Reference: 0.2–1.2 mg/dL)
• Direct Bilirubin: 2.4 mg/dL (Reference: 0.0–0.3 mg/dL)
• Serum Albumin: 2.7 g/dL (Reference: 3.5–5.0 g/dL)
• Serum Lactic Acid: 2.4 mmol/L (Reference: 0.5–2.0 mmol/L)
• Serum Sodium: 132 mEq/L (Reference: 135–145 mEq/L)
• Blood Alcohol Concentration: 85 mg/dL

Liver Core Biopsy & Electron Microscopy:
Biopsy demonstrates diffuse macrovesicular and microvesicular hepatic steatosis with lipid droplets compressing hepatocyte nuclei. Pronounced hydropic swelling (ballooning degeneration) is evident throughout centrilobular zones. Electron microscopy reveals dilated cisternae of the endoplasmic reticulum with detached ribosomes, swollen mitochondria, and plasma membrane surface blebs. Nuclear chromatin is preserved without fragmentation, and the basal lamina is intact. Upregulated ubiquitin-proteasome intermediates and chaperone stress proteins are detected.

• Total Bilirubin: 3.8 mg/dL (Reference: 0.2–1.2 mg/dL)
• Direct Bilirubin: 2.4 mg/dL (Reference: 0.0–0.3 mg/dL)
• Serum Albumin: 2.7 g/dL (Reference: 3.5–5.0 g/dL)
• Serum Lactic Acid: 2.4 mmol/L (Reference: 0.5–2.0 mmol/L)
• Serum Sodium: 132 mEq/L (Reference: 135–145 mEq/L)
• Blood Alcohol Concentration: 85 mg/dL

Liver Core Biopsy & Electron Microscopy:
Biopsy demonstrates diffuse macrovesicular and microvesicular hepatic steatosis with lipid droplets compressing hepatocyte nuclei. Pronounced hydropic swelling (ballooning degeneration) is evident throughout centrilobular zones. Electron microscopy reveals dilated cisternae of the endoplasmic reticulum with detached ribosomes, swollen mitochondria, and plasma membrane surface blebs. Nuclear chromatin is preserved without fragmentation, and the basal lamina is intact. Upregulated ubiquitin-proteasome intermediates and chaperone stress proteins are detected.

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 1400:Walter Henderson, a 72-year-old male, is admitted via EMS accompanied by his daughter. The daughter reports Walter has a 25-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, severe bilateral peripheral artery disease (PAD), and a remote coronary artery bypass graft. Over the past 3 weeks, he experienced severe, burning rest pain in his right forefoot that kept him awake at night, relieved only transiently by hanging his foot over the edge of the bed. Initially, his right second and third toes turned pale, cold, and numb, gradually becoming dark purple, and finally dry, shriveled, hard, and black with a sharp line of demarcation separating the dead tissue from healthy skin (dry gangrene). However, 48 hours ago, the black tissue softened, began weeping foul-smelling brown-yellow fluid, and the surrounding forefoot became swollen, red, and hot. On examination today, the nurse palpates distinct spongy, crackling sensations (subcutaneous crepitus) across the dorsum of the foot extending toward the ankle. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are non-palpable on the right (monophasic Doppler signal only). Client appears lethargic, diaphoretic, and shivering.

before.title: Laboratory & Wound Assessment
before.content:
Stat Laboratory Results:
• WBC: 21,400 /mm3 (Reference: 4,500–11,000) with 88% neutrophils, 10% band forms
• Hemoglobin: 10.8 g/dL (Reference: 13.5–17.5 g/dL)
• Serum Lactic Acid: 4.2 mmol/L (Reference: 0.5–2.0 mmol/L) [Tissue hypoperfusion]
• Serum Creatinine: 1.8 mg/dL (Baseline: 1.0 mg/dL) [Acute kidney injury]
• Blood Glucose: 312 mg/dL (Reference: 70–99 mg/dL)
• C-Reactive Protein (CRP): 145 mg/L (Reference: < 5 mg/L)

Gram Stain & Anaerobic Wound Smear:
Numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes; heavy growth of large Gram-positive, blunt-ended, spore-forming rods morphologically consistent with Clostridium perfringens, along with mixed Gram-negative enteric bacilli.

Right Foot Plain Radiograph (X-Ray):
Extensive soft tissue gas dissecting through the dorsal and plantar fascial compartments of the forefoot. Severe arterial calcification of dorsalis pedis and digital vessels. No bony osteomyelitis.

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 1200:(DOL1) Infant remains stable on room air. Pre- and post-ductal SpO2 remain 95–97%. Fed 20 mL of expressed breast milk via specialty Haberman feeder with frequent rest periods due to weak suck and tongue protrusion; no emesis or coughing noted during feed. Cardiac murmur unchanged. Mother expresses grief and anxiety regarding the preliminary diagnosis of Down syndrome and asks questions regarding how sex chromosome disorders differ from autosomal disorders.

before.title: Diagnostic & Genetic Reports
before.content:
Neonatal Echocardiogram Report (1000):
Normal left ventricular systolic function (EF 64%). Large ostium primum atrial septal defect (ASD) measuring 6.2 mm with left-to-right shunt. Mild mitral valve regurgitation without outflow tract obstruction. Pulmonary arterial pressures estimated at upper limits of normal for transitional neonatal circulation. Follow-up pediatric cardiology consultation scheduled.
Rapid Fluorescent In Situ Hybridization (FISH) & Karyotype (1130):
Karyotype result: 47,XY,+21. Three distinct copies of chromosome 21 identified in all 20 metaphase cells examined, confirming non-mosaic complete Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome). Sex chromosomes: XY (genotypically male).

after.title: Nurses' Notes
after.content:
0100:Day-of-Life 1 (DOL1). Term male infant admitted from labor and delivery for transition monitoring. Birth weight: 3,120 g (40th percentile); length: 48 cm (35th percentile); head circumference: 32 cm (25th percentile). Maternal history: 41-year-old G3P3, prenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks noted thickened nuchal fold, but parents declined definitive prenatal amniocentesis. Infant is awake but exhibits marked generalized muscular hypotonia ('floppy infant' appearance) with poor resistance to passive elbow and knee extension. Facial exam notable for brachycephaly with a flattened occiput, flattened nasal bridge, prominent epicanthal folds with upslanting eyes, and small low-set ears. Oral exam demonstrates a protruding tongue that pushes against the nipple, causing difficulty latching during initial bottle-feeding attempt. Hands exhibit short, broad fingers with a single continuous transverse flexion crease across both palms. Auscultation reveals a grade 3/6 harsh pansystolic murmur audible at the lower left sternal border without heave. Peripheral pulses +2 bilaterally. Couple asks detailed questions: 'If our first baby is born with Cystic Fibrosis, does that mean our next three children are guaranteed to be healthy?' Couple also inquires about the difference between being a healthy carrier of a recessive gene versus having a dominant gene like Marfan syndrome. David expresses urgent concern regarding his own aortic root dilation and sudden death risk.

before.title: Punnett Probability Reference
before.content:
Mendelian Risk Summary:

  • Autosomal Recessive (Carrier x Carrier): 25% affected (homozygous), 50% carrier (heterozygous), 25% uninfected non-carrier.
  • Autosomal Dominant (Affected Heterozygote x Unaffected): 50% affected, 50% unaffected; equal risk for males and females.
  • X-Linked Recessive (Carrier Mother x Normal Father): 50% of sons affected; 50% of daughters are carriers; no sons receive father's X.

before.title: Teratology Principles Chart
before.content:
Principles of Teratology:

  • Pre-implantation (Day 0–14): 'All-or-none' phenomenon (lethal damage or complete recovery without malformation).
  • Embryonic Period (Weeks 3–8): Peak susceptibility to major structural anomalies across all organ systems (CNS, heart, limbs, eyes, palate).
  • Fetal Period (Week 9 to Term): Susceptibility to functional defects, growth restriction, and microcephaly.
  • Multifactorial Threshold: Combined gene-environment interactions govern liability to defects like cleft lip/palate.

before.title: Clinical Pathway
before.content:
Interprofessional Care Plan:

  • Neonatal Feeding: Upright positioning, cleft palate bottle, burp q15–30 mL, strict aspiration precautions.
  • Infection Control / CMV: Standard precautions (CMV shedding in saliva and urine; pregnant healthcare staff must avoid direct urine/saliva contact). IV ganciclovir per protocol.
  • Hematology: Daily CBC to monitor platelets; avoid IM injections while platelets < 100 × 109/L.
  • Plastic Surgery / Craniofacial: Consult for cleft lip repair timeline (typically rule of 10s: 10 weeks, 10 lbs, Hb 10 g/dL).

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 1130:Pathology reports received and reviewed with client and surgical oncologist. The client asks: 'How can I have a lump in my uterus that is safe, but a lump in my breast that is life-threatening? What makes them so different?' Nurse prepares to provide clear pathophysiological education regarding benign versus malignant cellular behavior, tissue differentiation, and metastatic mechanisms.

before.title: Diagnostic & Pathology Reports
before.content:
Pelvic Ultrasound Summary (Uterine Lesion):
5.2 × 4.8 cm sharply demarcated intramural mass in posterior uterine wall. Hypoechoic, uniform echotexture enclosed within a distinct fibrous pseudocapsule. No invasion of endometrium or serosa. Appearance consistent with benign uterine leiomyoma (fibroid).
Right Breast Core Needle Biopsy Pathology (Breast Mass):
Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (Adenocarcinoma). High histologic grade (Grade 3). Markedly anaplastic epithelial cells forming disordered sheets with absence of gland formation. Prominent cellular pleomorphism, frequent atypical mitotic figures, and central areas of coagulative tumor necrosis. High degree of lymphatic channel invasion noted within the stroma. Receptor status: Estrogen Receptor (ER) positive (80%), Progesterone Receptor (PR) positive (65%), HER2/neu negative (IHC 1+).

after.title: Nurses' Notes
after.content:
0830:Eleanor Vance, a 46-year-old female (G2P2), presents for evaluation. Gynecological history: has had a known uterine mass for 6 years, monitored by serial ultrasound, which produces menorrhagia (heavy menses) and mild lower abdominal pressure. Pelvic ultrasound from last week shows a 5.2 cm well-circumscribed, smoothly encapsulated intramural uterine leiomyoma with no abnormal vascularity or pelvic lymphadenopathy. Over the past 10 weeks, however, the client discovered a distinct, rapidly enlarging lump in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. On inspection, there is subtle right nipple retraction and slight erythema with a 'peau d'orange' pitted skin texture over the right upper breast. On palpation, the breast mass is approximately 3.5 cm in diameter, stony hard, irregular, and immobile (fixed to underlying chest wall). Palpation of the right axilla reveals two enlarged, firm, non-tender lymph nodes measuring ~1.5 cm that feel matted together. Left breast and axilla are normal. Client reports feeling fatigued and notes an unintentional weight loss of 6 kg over the past 2 months. Vital signs stable. Nurse prepares client for diagnostic imaging and biopsy.

1130:Pathology reports received and reviewed with client and surgical oncologist. The client asks: 'How can I have a lump in my uterus that is safe, but a lump in my breast that is life-threatening? What makes them so different?' Nurse prepares to provide clear pathophysiological education regarding benign versus malignant cellular behavior, tissue differentiation, and metastatic mechanisms.

before.title: Surgical Consult Plan

Frozen section analysis will be performed intraoperatively. If sentinel node is negative, axilla is preserved. If sentinel node shows macrometastatic burden, axillary management will follow standard staging protocol.

after.title: Nurses' Notes
after.content:
0830:Eleanor Vance, a 46-year-old female (G2P2), presents for evaluation. Gynecological history: has had a known uterine mass for 6 years, monitored by serial ultrasound, which produces menorrhagia (heavy menses) and mild lower abdominal pressure. Pelvic ultrasound from last week shows a 5.2 cm well-circumscribed, smoothly encapsulated intramural uterine leiomyoma with no abnormal vascularity or pelvic lymphadenopathy. Over the past 10 weeks, however, the client discovered a distinct, rapidly enlarging lump in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. On inspection, there is subtle right nipple retraction and slight erythema with a 'peau d'orange' pitted skin texture over the right upper breast. On palpation, the breast mass is approximately 3.5 cm in diameter, stony hard, irregular, and immobile (fixed to underlying chest wall). Palpation of the right axilla reveals two enlarged, firm, non-tender lymph nodes measuring ~1.5 cm that feel matted together. Left breast and axilla are normal. Client reports feeling fatigued and notes an unintentional weight loss of 6 kg over the past 2 months. Vital signs stable. Nurse prepares client for diagnostic imaging and biopsy.

1130:Pathology reports received and reviewed with client and surgical oncologist. The client asks: 'How can I have a lump in my uterus that is safe, but a lump in my breast that is life-threatening? What makes them so different?' Nurse prepares to provide clear pathophysiological education regarding benign versus malignant cellular behavior, tissue differentiation, and metastatic mechanisms.

Client expresses anxiety regarding arm swelling: 'My friend had breast surgery 10 years ago and had terrible arm lymphedema because they took all 20 lymph nodes out. Will that happen to me?' Nurse explains the role of sentinel lymph node identification using dye/tracer, explaining that only the first 1 to 3 guardian nodes are biopsied first to avoid unnecessary complete axillary dissection.

1430:Preoperative education conducted. Client actively engages in discussion and asks detailed questions regarding the blue dye mapping and surgical incisions. Client verbalizes understanding that the uterine leiomyoma is benign and does not require urgent surgery, while the breast carcinoma is the primary medical priority. Written educational pamphlets on sentinel node mapping and postoperative wound care provided.

after.title: Diagnostic & Pathology Reports
after.content:
Pelvic Ultrasound Summary (Uterine Lesion):
5.2 × 4.8 cm sharply demarcated intramural mass in posterior uterine wall. Hypoechoic, uniform echotexture enclosed within a distinct fibrous pseudocapsule. No invasion of endometrium or serosa. Appearance consistent with benign uterine leiomyoma (fibroid).
Right Breast Core Needle Biopsy Pathology (Breast Mass):
Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (Adenocarcinoma). High histologic grade (Grade 3). Markedly anaplastic epithelial cells forming disordered sheets with absence of gland formation. Prominent cellular pleomorphism, frequent atypical mitotic figures, and central areas of coagulative tumor necrosis. High degree of lymphatic channel invasion noted within the stroma. Receptor status: Estrogen Receptor (ER) positive (80%), Progesterone Receptor (PR) positive (65%), HER2/neu negative (IHC 1+).

Full axillary dissection avoided. Discharge teaching initiated with client and spouse.

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 1330:Colonoscopy completed under moderate procedural sedation. Findings: large, friable, ulcerating, semi-obstructing annular lesion at 30 cm from the anal verge in the sigmoid colon. Biopsies obtained. Multiple synchronous tubular adenomatous polyps in the descending colon successfully excised via snare polypectomy. Client tolerated procedure well, transferred to recovery, awake and alert. Surgical oncology consultation scheduled.

before.title: Diagnostic & Endoscopy Reports
before.content:
Endoscopy Report (Colonoscopy):
Sigmoid Colon: Circumferential mass measuring 4.2 cm in length causing ~70% lumen narrowing. Lumen traversed with pediatric colonoscope with care. Biopsies × 6 obtained. Descending colon: Two peduncular polyps (1.0 cm and 0.8 cm) removed completely by cold snare.
Molecular & Pathology Summary:
Sigmoid Biopsy: Moderately differentiated invasive Adenocarcinoma. Molecular sequencing: Point mutation in K-Ras codon 12 (activating mutation). Homozygous deletion of APC gene and missense mutation in TP53 (loss of functional p53 protein). Telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) promoter mutation detected.

after.title: Nurses' Notes
after.content:
0900:Robert Chen, a 61-year-old male, presents for consultation. He participated in a routine provincial colorectal cancer screening program 3 weeks ago; his Fecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) was reported positive for human hemoglobin (185 ng/mL; normal < 20 ng/mL). History: reports that over the past 4 months, he has noticed progressive constipation alternating with loose, pencil-thin stools, accompanied by intermittent cramping in the left lower abdominal quadrant. He notes maroon-streaked stools on multiple occasions. Denies previous colonoscopy. Social history: 40 pack-year cigarette smoking history (1 pack/day for 40 years), sedentary desk job, diet predominantly composed of processed red meats, cured sausages, and fast foods, with minimal fruit/vegetable intake. BMI: 31.4 kg/m² (Class I Obesity). Reports chronic fatigue and exertional shortness of breath when walking up hills. Laboratory workup reveals microcytic anemia. Colonoscopy scheduled for tomorrow morning.

1330:Colonoscopy completed under moderate procedural sedation. Findings: large, friable, ulcerating, semi-obstructing annular lesion at 30 cm from the anal verge in the sigmoid colon. Biopsies obtained. Multiple synchronous tubular adenomatous polyps in the descending colon successfully excised via snare polypectomy. Client tolerated procedure well, transferred to recovery, awake and alert. Surgical oncology consultation scheduled.

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 1500:Post-procedure debriefing with Robert and his spouse. Robert expresses confusion: 'I thought colon cancer was just a bad polyp. How did genes like p53 and K-Ras cause this?' Nurse explains how normal cells gradually accumulate genetic 'hits'—a switch turning on growth (oncogene K-Ras) and broken brakes (loss of tumor suppressors APC and p53)—eventually leading to an immortal, invasive mass. Couple expresses readiness to discuss treatment and prevention of future recurrences.

Lesion 1 (nasal ala): shows classic arborizing telangiectatic vessels, shiny white structures, and blue-gray ovoid nests diagnostic of Basal Cell Carcinoma. before.title: Dermatological Reference
before.content:
Dermatological Morphological Principles:
• Primary Lesions: Macule, Patch, Papule, Plaque, Nodule, Tumor, Wheal, Vesicle, Bulla, Pustule.
• Secondary Lesions: Scale, Crust, Erosion, Ulcer, Fissure, Lichenification, Atrophy, Excoriation, Scar, Keloid.
Age-Related Histology: Thinning epidermis, flattening of dermoepidermal rete ridges (susceptibility to skin shearing/tears), decreased collagen and fragmented elastin (wrinkling/sagging), reduced dermal vascular beds with fragile capillary loops (senile purpura), and decreased sebum (xerosis).

after.title: Nurses' Notes
after.content:
0900:Harold Jenkins, a 74-year-old male, presents for evaluation of long-standing skin changes and two 'troublesome spots'. Occupational history: worked outdoors as an agricultural farmer and landscaper for over 50 years, rarely used sunscreen or protective clothing. Medical history: hypertension, osteoarthritis. Integumentary inspection: generalized severe photoaging with yellowed, furrowed 'weather-beaten' skin texture across face and neck. Bilateral dorsal forearms exhibit multiple flat, non-blanching violaceous patches (actinic/senile purpura) without hematoma. Lesion 1 (Nose): On the right nasal ala, there is a 6 mm discrete, pearly, translucent pinkish papule with central indentation and fine arborizing telangiectatic vessels; client states it bleeds whenever he washes his face. Lesion 2 (Upper Back): In the left infrascapular region, there is an 8 mm pigmented lesion; spouse noticed it 4 months ago and states it has darkened and expanded. Inspection reveals marked asymmetry, irregular notched margins, and mixed colors (tan, dark brown, jet black, and bluish-red foci). Palpation of the left axilla reveals a single firm, non-tender, mobile 1.5 cm lymph node. Client denies weight loss or bone pain. Vital signs stable. Biopsy planned.

before.title: Pathology Reports
before.content:
Specimen A (Right Nasal Ala):
Nodular Basal Cell Carcinoma. Islands of atypical basaloid epithelial cells with peripheral palisading and clefting artifact. Stroma exhibits telangiectatic capillaries. Lateral margins clear; deep margin transects tumor. Recommendation: Mohs micrographic surgery.
Specimen B (Left Upper Back):
Malignant Melanoma (Superficial Spreading). Breslow depth: 1.8 mm. Ulceration: Present. Mitotic index: 3/mm². Microscopic satellite lesions: None. Vascular/lymphatic invasion: Equivocal. Margin: Positive at peripheral ink. Pathologic Stage: pT2b. Recommendation: Wide re-excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy.

Bilateral dorsal forearms exhibit multiple flat, non-blanching violaceous patches (actinic/senile purpura) without hematoma. Lesion 1 (Nose): On the right nasal ala, there is a 6 mm discrete, pearly, translucent pinkish papule with central indentation and fine arborizing telangiectatic vessels; client states it bleeds whenever he washes his face. Lesion 2 (Upper Back): In the left infrascapular region, there is an 8 mm pigmented lesion; spouse noticed it 4 months ago and states it has darkened and expanded. Inspection reveals marked asymmetry, irregular notched margins, and mixed colors (tan, dark brown, jet black, and bluish-red foci). Palpation of the left axilla reveals a single firm, non-tender, mobile 1.5 cm lymph node. Client denies weight loss or bone pain. Vital signs stable. Biopsy planned.

1000:Dermatoscopic examination performed by dermatologist. Lesion 1 (nasal ala): shows classic arborizing telangiectatic vessels, shiny white structures, and blue-gray ovoid nests diagnostic of Basal Cell Carcinoma. Lesion 2 (upper back): dermatoscopy reveals atypical pigment network, irregular globules, and blue-white veil highly suspicious for invasive Malignant Melanoma. Shave biopsy performed on nasal lesion; complete full-thickness excisional biopsy with 2 mm clinical margins performed on upper back lesion. Client tolerated procedures well. Biopsy specimens sent for histopathology.

1400 (4 days post-biopsy):Pathology review: Lesion 1 (nose) confirmed Nodular Basal Cell Carcinoma; deep margin involved; scheduled for Mohs micrographic surgery for tissue preservation. Lesion 2 (upper back) confirmed Invasive Malignant Melanoma, superficial spreading subtype, Breslow depth 1.8 mm (intermediate thickness, Clark level IV), ulceration present, 3 mitoses/mm². Deep and peripheral surgical margins positive for melanoma in situ. Wide local excision with 2 cm margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy scheduled. Nurse reviews findings and care plan with Harold and his spouse.

1500:Education session conducted. Harold verbalizes surprise that his decades of farming without a shirt contributed to both his easy bruising (senile purpura) and the malignant melanoma on his back. Nurse reviews the ABCDE self-examination guide and provides photographic examples. Harold's spouse agrees to inspect his back monthly. Sun-safety strategies (sunscreen, UV-protective long-sleeved clothing, wide-brimmed hat) and gentle skin barrier hygiene reinforced.

1000 (Post-Op Day 2):Surgical incisions evaluated. Right nasal reconstruction flap is pink, viable, capillary refill < 2 seconds, sutures intact without hematoma. Left back surgical wound has 6 cm linear suture line; dressing removed with gentle silicone adhesive remover; no skin tears noted on fragile surrounding skin. Incision clean, dry, well-approximated, mild erythema limited to incision margin. Pain rated 2/10 on acetaminophen. Client verbalizes restriction on heavy farm work for 2 weeks.

1100 (Post-Op Day 10):Sutures removed from right nose and upper back; incisions healed with clean, flat scars. Pathology of wide local re-excision: margins completely clear of melanoma (> 2 cm margins). Sentinel lymph node biopsy of left axilla: 2 nodes examined, both negative for metastatic melanoma (0/2; pN0). Stage confirmed Stage IIA (pT2b N0 M0). No adjuvant therapy indicated at this time. Scheduled for dermatologic full-body skin exam every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months. Harold and his spouse demonstrate excellent comprehension of skin protection strategies.

after.title: Dermatological Reference
after.content:
Dermatological Morphological Principles:
• Primary Lesions: Macule, Patch, Papule, Plaque, Nodule, Tumor, Wheal, Vesicle, Bulla, Pustule.
• Secondary Lesions: Scale, Crust, Erosion, Ulcer, Fissure, Lichenification, Atrophy, Excoriation, Scar, Keloid.
Age-Related Histology: Thinning epidermis, flattening of dermoepidermal rete ridges (susceptibility to skin shearing/tears), decreased collagen and fragmented elastin (wrinkling/sagging), reduced dermal vascular beds with fragile capillary loops (senile purpura), and decreased sebum (xerosis).

after.title: Pathology Reports
after.content:
Specimen A (Right Nasal Ala):
Nodular Basal Cell Carcinoma. Islands of atypical basaloid epithelial cells with peripheral palisading and clefting artifact. Stroma exhibits telangiectatic capillaries. Lateral margins clear; deep margin transects tumor. Recommendation: Mohs micrographic surgery.
Specimen B (Left Upper Back):
Malignant Melanoma (Superficial Spreading). Breslow depth: 1.8 mm. Ulceration: Present. Mitotic index: 3/mm². Microscopic satellite lesions: None. Vascular/lymphatic invasion: Equivocal. Margin: Positive at peripheral ink. Pathologic Stage: pT2b. Recommendation: Wide re-excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy.

Primary survey (CAB/ABC): Airway: client is awake, speaking in a raspy, strained whisper. Facial burns present; eyebrows and nasal hairs completely singed. Oral cavity inspection reveals carbonaceous soot on hard palate, posterior pharynx, and uvula, with mild edematous swelling of the buccal mucosa. Auscultation of the trachea reveals audible high-pitched inspiratory stridor; bilateral lung fields exhibit scattered expiratory wheezes. Breathing: tachypneic at 28 breaths/min; 100% non-rebreather mask applied. Circulation: peripheral pulses thready at 124 bpm; blood pressure 98/62 mmHg. Severe burns covering the anterior torso and bilateral entire upper extremities with mixed areas of blistered red dermis and dry, waxy, leathery eschar. Neurological: GCS 14 (confused, anxious from hypoxia and pain). Trauma team alerted for immediate rapid sequence intubation.

0915:Endotracheal intubation performed smoothly by trauma team prior to worsening laryngeal edema; tube secured at 23 cm at teeth. Mechanical ventilation initiated on 100% FiO2 with lung-protective settings. Burn mapping verified: face (4.5%), anterior chest/abdomen (18%), right upper extremity circumference (9%), left upper extremity circumference (9%), totaling 40.5% TBSA (partial- and full-thickness). Total weight: 80 kg. Foley catheter placed, initial output 15 mL of dark, concentrated amber urine. Stat laboratory values received. Parkland resuscitation calculations initiated.

0930:Parkland fluid resuscitation active: 12,960 mL total LR planned for first 24 hours. Prehospital EMS infused 500 mL LR over 45 minutes; remaining first 8-hour requirement is 5,980 mL over the next 7 hours and 15 minutes (~825 mL/hr across two large-bore peripheral IV lines). Hourly Foley urometer measurements initiated. Core temperature maintained at 37.0 °C with overhead radiant warmers and warm blankets. Burn wounds covered with clean, dry, sterile sheets; topical antimicrobials deferred until primary trauma survey and fluid resuscitation are stabilized.

1130 (Hour 3 Post-Injury):Tyler remains sedated and intubated on mechanical ventilation. Endotracheal suctioning yields moderate amount of soot-tinged mucus; bilateral breath sounds clear with scattered rhonchi. IV LR infusing at 825 mL/hr. Foley output over the past hour was 42 mL (0.52 mL/kg/hr, on target). Blood pressure: 104/66 mmHg, HR 110 bpm. Telemetry shows sinus tachycardia with narrow QRS and normal T waves. Ambient room temperature maintained at 31 °C; patient's core temperature is 36.8 °C. Clean dry dressings intact.

1445 (Hour 6 Post-Injury):Resuscitation parameters: Urine output for the past hour was 48 mL (cumulative 6-hour output: 245 mL, avg 41 mL/hr). Blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, HR 102 bpm. Bilateral radial pulses assessed via Doppler ultrasound: strong biphasic acoustic signals present; brisk capillary refill in nailbeds. Upper extremities elevated on pillows to promote venous return. Serum potassium trending down from 5.8 to 5.1 mmol/L; hematocrit stabilized at 48%. Lactate decreased to 2.4 mmol/L. Total LR infused in first 6 hours: 4,800 mL. On schedule to complete first half by Hour 8.

1500 (Hour 30 Post-Burn):Tyler has entered the diuretic phase. Spontaneous urine output has increased to 75–90 mL/hr. IV Lactated Ringer's infusion successfully stepped down to maintenance D5 0.45% NS with 20 mEq KCl/L. Serum sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L (hypokalemia monitored and replaced), hematocrit 36% (hemodilution). Arterial blood gas shows PaO2 98 mmHg on FiO2 40% with PEEP 5 cm H2O. Weaning protocol initiated. Burn surgery team scheduled Tyler for tangential excision and autografting of deep partial-thickness arm burns tomorrow.

before.title: Nurses' Notes
before.content: 1620:Burn surgeon arrives at bedside. Right calf compartment pressure measured with Stryker needle: 38 mmHg (abnormally elevated; normal < 10–15 mmHg; > 30 mmHg diagnostic of compartment syndrome). Right dorsalis pedis Doppler signal has completely ceased. Immediate bedside escharotomy performed under sterile conditions: longitudinal medial and lateral incisions made through the rigid, insensate eschar of the right lower leg down to subcutaneous fat. Upon incision, the eschar edges immediately gape open by 1.5 cm with visible decompression of underlying tissues. Bleeding controlled with electrocautery. Within 5 minutes, Doppler acoustic signal returns strongly in dorsalis pedis artery; toes become warm with capillary refill < 2 seconds. Pain on passive stretch diminishes. Sterile non-adherent dressings applied.

before.title: Wound Healing Stages Reference
before.content:
Four Phases of Natural Wound Healing in Burns:
  • Phase 1: Hemostasis: Platelet aggregation, fibrin clot formation, provisional matrix.
  • Phase 2: Inflammation: Neutrophil and macrophage infiltration, cytokine release (VEGF, TGF-β, PDGF), clearing debris/bacteria.
  • Phase 3: Proliferation: Fibroblast migration, collagen deposition, angiogenesis, epithelialization.
  • Phase 4: Remodeling: Collagen cross-linking, matrix remodeling by MMPs, scar contracture maturation.
